matrix.title: Matrix
matrix.one_liner: Matrix is an artificial society simulation where each node in a graph is powered by its own LLM agent with memory, personality, and goals.
matrix.full_summary: I built Matrix as an artificial society simulation rather than a single-agent demo. Each node in the graph is its own LLM-powered agent with memory, personality, and goals, and a larger orchestrator model manages task assignment, interactions, and the spread of information across the network.
matrix.why_it_matters: Matrix matters to me because it lets me work on the systems side of AI: orchestration, memory, multi-agent behavior, external tools, and how local interactions create larger network-level dynamics.
matrix.problem: Most AI interfaces stop at one model talking to one user. I wanted to simulate what happens when many persistent agents interact inside a structured social graph and information moves between them over time.
matrix.solution: I built a graph-based simulation with smaller per-agent models, a larger central orchestrator, persistent memory, and external data access. Users can also join the simulation directly through avatar-based real-time video calls.
matrix.your_role: I designed the multi-agent architecture, built the orchestration flow, handled memory and external tool integration, and connected the system to avatar-based real-time interaction.
highlights: Built an artificial society where each graph node is its own LLM-powered agent.
Used a larger orchestrator model to assign tasks and manage interactions between agents.
Maintained persistent context with memory systems so agents could evolve over time.
Pulled in outside information through external APIs and web data sources.
Let users insert themselves into the simulation through real-time avatar video calls.
architecture: A graph of agents where each node has its own local context, personality, and goals.
Smaller models run per agent while a larger reasoning model coordinates global behavior.
Memory systems preserve context and influence future interactions.
External tools supply fresh information that can propagate through the simulated society.
Avatar and video interfaces allow humans to interact with agents directly.
challenges: Keeping many agents coherent without collapsing everything into one centralized model.
Managing cost and latency across GPU-hosted inference.
Designing interactions that feel socially structured instead of random.
Blending simulation behavior with real-time human interaction.
tradeoffs: Using smaller per-agent models improves scale, but it puts more pressure on orchestration.
Persistent memory makes the simulation richer, but also makes consistency harder.
Adding real-time avatar interaction makes the system more compelling, but increases infrastructure complexity.
results: Built a working multi-agent society simulation with persistent memory and real-time human interaction.

faq.answer: Matrix is my artificial society simulation. Each node is its own LLM agent, and a larger orchestrator manages how agents interact and how information spreads.

adapt-ui.title: Adapt UI
adapt-ui.one_liner: Adapt UI turns natural language prompts into fully functional React components through a generate, validate, and repair pipeline.
adapt-ui.full_summary: I built Adapt UI as a system for turning natural language into working React components instead of stopping at one-shot code generation. The pipeline has separate stages for generation, validation, and repair, and it runs generated code in a sandboxed environment so the focus stays on reliability and actual renderability.
adapt-ui.why_it_matters: Adapt UI matters to me because it is about making LLM output dependable. I wanted to build a system that cares about whether generated UI actually compiles and renders, not just whether it looks plausible in a demo.
adapt-ui.problem: AI-generated UI often looks impressive at first, but fails on imports, props, types, or runtime behavior when you try to actually use it.
adapt-ui.solution: I built a multi-stage loop where one model generates code, another validates it, and a third tries to repair failures using structured error context from the sandboxed execution environment.
adapt-ui.your_role: I designed the pipeline, implemented validation and repair loops, handled sandboxing constraints, and focused on improving prompt-to-render reliability.
highlights: Built a multi-stage generate, validate, and repair pipeline for React components.
Ran generated code inside a sandboxed environment with restricted capabilities.
Used structured validation feedback instead of relying on a single-shot generation pass.
Optimized for reliability and actual rendering, not just code generation.
architecture: Stage 1 turns a natural-language prompt into a React component.
Stage 2 validates the output against compile and runtime constraints.
Stage 3 uses structured failure context to repair the component.
The loop repeats within a bounded budget to improve render success without running forever.
challenges: Generated code can fail in subtle ways even when it looks correct.
Compiler and runtime errors have to be translated into useful repair context.
Tighter constraints improve reliability, but they can also narrow what the model is willing to generate.
tradeoffs: More validation improves reliability, but adds latency.
Sandboxing improves safety, but limits what the generated code can do.
Bounded repair loops prevent runaway retries, but they can stop before a perfect fix.
results: Improved prompt-to-render reliability by using iterative generate, validate, and repair loops instead of a single pass.

faq.answer: Adapt UI is my system for turning prompts into React components. It uses generate, validate, and repair loops so the output is more likely to actually compile and render.

robintrain.title: RobinTrain
robintrain.one_liner: RobinTrain is an AI training system for simulating customer support interactions and evaluating support behavior.
robintrain.full_summary: I built RobinTrain as an AI training system for customer support workflows. It simulates both sides of support conversations, creates dynamic scenarios, and helps companies train or evaluate support performance in situations that feel less scripted and more like real-world interactions.
robintrain.why_it_matters: RobinTrain matters to me because it applies conversational AI to a real operational workflow. The interesting part is not just generating dialogue, but making the scenarios realistic enough to expose edge cases and training gaps.
robintrain.problem: Support organizations need better ways to simulate realistic customer interactions, test edge cases, and evaluate how support systems and agents perform under different conditions.
robintrain.solution: I built a simulation system that models both users and support agents, generates dynamic conversation flows, and creates less scripted support scenarios for training and evaluation.
robintrain.your_role: I designed the simulation flow, modeled both sides of the support conversation, and focused on realism, variability, and evaluation value.
highlights: Simulated both customers and support agents inside the same system.
Generated dynamic support scenarios instead of relying on fixed scripts.
Used the system for edge-case testing and workflow evaluation.
Focused on realism so the conversations feel closer to real support interactions.
architecture: A simulation layer models conversation state and scenario progression.
LLM-based actors generate user and support-side responses.
Evaluation logic can inspect the conversation for training or benchmarking purposes.
Prompt design drives realism, variability, and behavior under stress cases.
challenges: Making simulated users feel realistic instead of repetitive.
Balancing variability with enough structure for evaluation.
Ensuring the generated scenarios are useful for real training workflows.
tradeoffs: More realistic simulations increase complexity and prompt design overhead.
Tighter control makes evaluation easier, but can make conversations feel scripted.
Open-ended dialogue improves realism, but makes scoring and benchmarking harder.
results: Built a realistic support conversation simulator for training, edge-case testing, and evaluation.

faq.answer: RobinTrain is my AI support training system. It simulates both sides of customer support conversations so teams can train on more realistic scenarios and edge cases.

aura-dev.title: Aura Dev
aura-dev.one_liner: Aura Dev is a voice-first coding assistant that lets developers interact with code entirely through speech.
aura-dev.full_summary: I built Aura Dev as a voice-first coding assistant that connects spoken input to real coding workflows. It captures speech, converts it to text, interprets intent, and executes actions through a coding agent that can modify files, run commands, and respond with text-to-speech.
aura-dev.why_it_matters: Aura Dev matters to me because it combines the exact kinds of systems problems I like most: live audio, orchestration, execution tools, and making the interface between language and real work feel low-friction.
aura-dev.problem: Most coding assistants are still built around text chat, which makes them less natural for hands-free or live interaction with development workflows.
aura-dev.solution: I built a pipeline that connects real-time speech-to-text, LLM orchestration, CLI-based coding tools, and text-to-speech so developers can drive code workflows by talking.
aura-dev.your_role: I designed and built the end-to-end voice pipeline, from speech capture through orchestration and coding-agent execution.
highlights: Built a voice-first interface for coding workflows.
Connected speech input to intent interpretation and CLI-based execution.
Used real-time STT and TTS to keep the interaction fast and natural.
Made it possible to modify files, run commands, and get spoken feedback.
architecture: Speech is captured and streamed into a real-time STT pipeline.
An orchestration layer interprets the spoken request and maps it to an action.
A coding agent executes commands and edits through CLI tools.
Text-to-speech closes the loop with spoken responses.
challenges: Speech is naturally less precise than typed commands, so intent handling has to be robust.
Latency compounds quickly when STT, orchestration, execution, and TTS are all in the loop.
Execution needs to feel capable without becoming unsafe or brittle.
tradeoffs: Voice-first interaction lowers friction, but it also increases ambiguity.
Real-time feedback makes the system feel natural, but it raises latency pressure across the stack.
Deeper execution capabilities are powerful, but they require tighter orchestration and safety controls.
results: Built a working voice-native coding assistant that connects spoken language to real development actions.

faq.answer: Aura Dev is my voice-first coding assistant. It turns speech into coding actions by combining real-time STT, orchestration, CLI execution, and TTS.

elbow-exo.title: Elbow Exo
elbow-exo.one_liner: Elbow Exo is a real-time biomechanical tracking system that estimates elbow flexion using dual IMU sensors.
elbow-exo.full_summary: I built Elbow Exo as a real-time biomechanical tracking system centered on estimating elbow joint angles from dual IMU sensors. The system streams motion data over BLE, processes it continuously, and applies sensor-fusion logic to produce stable elbow flexion estimates that can be visualized or analyzed downstream.
elbow-exo.why_it_matters: Elbow Exo matters to me because it sits right at the intersection of hardware, signal processing, and real-time software, which is where I like working most.
elbow-exo.problem: Raw IMU data is noisy and drifts over time, so estimating joint angles accurately in a real-time streaming setting is harder than just reading the sensor values.
elbow-exo.solution: I built a dual-sensor pipeline that streams over BLE, fuses accelerometer and gyroscope data, filters noise and drift, and computes elbow flexion angles in real time.
elbow-exo.your_role: I worked on the streaming, estimation, and real-time processing pipeline for joint-angle tracking.
highlights: Streamed motion data from dual IMU sensors over BLE.
Estimated elbow flexion angles continuously in real time.
Used sensor-fusion and filtering techniques to reduce noise and drift.
Focused on latency, stability, and accuracy in a continuous pipeline.
architecture: Two IMU sensors stream accelerometer and gyroscope data.
BLE transport moves the sensor data into the processing pipeline.
Sensor-fusion logic combines signals to estimate joint angle more robustly.
Filtering stages stabilize the output for real-time visualization or downstream use.
challenges: IMU drift can accumulate quickly in continuous motion tracking.
Noise and movement artifacts make angle estimation unstable if the pipeline is too naive.
Low latency matters because the output is meant to feel real-time.
tradeoffs: Heavier filtering improves stability, but can hurt responsiveness.
A more reactive estimate feels better in real time, but can become noisier.
BLE streaming keeps the setup lightweight, but it also adds communication constraints.
results: Built a real-time elbow-angle tracking pipeline based on dual IMU streaming and sensor fusion.

faq.answer: Elbow Exo is my real-time elbow tracking project. It uses dual IMUs, BLE streaming, and sensor fusion to estimate elbow flexion accurately and with low latency.

gymbro.title: GymBro
gymbro.one_liner: GymBro is a mobile app that matches users with compatible gym partners based on goals, preferences, and schedules.
gymbro.full_summary: I built GymBro as a fitness-focused mobile app for matching people with compatible gym partners. The idea is to combine user goals, preferences, and scheduling information with messaging and matching logic so coordinating workouts feels simple instead of awkward.
gymbro.why_it_matters: GymBro matters to me because it connects a personal interest of mine, fitness, with consumer product design and matching logic.
gymbro.problem: Finding a consistent gym partner is usually informal and inconvenient, even though compatibility around goals, schedule, and training style matters a lot.
gymbro.solution: I built a mobile app with user profiles, matching logic, messaging, and a lightweight social layer to make finding and coordinating with a gym partner easier.
gymbro.your_role: I designed the product around matchmaking, profile data, messaging, and a simple mobile experience.
highlights: Matched users based on fitness goals, preferences, and schedules.
Built profile, messaging, and coordination flows into the app.
Focused on usability so the social side of working out feels lightweight.
Connected a consumer mobile interface to real-time messaging and matching logic.
architecture: User profiles capture fitness goals, preferences, and schedule signals.
A matching layer ranks compatibility between potential gym partners.
Firebase handles backend storage and real-time messaging flows.
The mobile frontend keeps coordination and conversation simple.
challenges: Compatibility is subjective, so the matching logic has to stay useful without feeling rigid.
Messaging and coordination matter just as much as the initial match.
The app has to feel social without turning into a heavy social network.
tradeoffs: More profile detail can improve matching, but it also raises onboarding friction.
Simple matching feels lightweight, but can miss nuance around compatibility.
A richer social layer can improve retention, but it also increases product complexity.
results: Built a social fitness app focused on gym-partner matching and real-time coordination.

faq.answer: GymBro is my gym-partner matching app. It uses profiles, preferences, schedules, and messaging to help users find compatible workout partners.

apollo.title: Apollo
apollo.one_liner: Apollo is a generative visual system focused on structure, symmetry, and mathematically controlled motion.
apollo.full_summary: I built Apollo as a generative visual system centered on structure, symmetry, and precision. The interactions are meant to feel deliberate and controlled, with visuals driven by geometric rules and rhythmic motion rather than organic chaos.
apollo.why_it_matters: Apollo matters to me because it explores a more ordered side of interactive visuals, where elegance comes from constraint and mathematical structure.
apollo.problem: Many generative visuals prioritize spectacle over control. I wanted to build something where the output feels clean, balanced, and intentionally constructed.
apollo.solution: I designed a visual system around symmetry, geometry, and tightly controlled motion so the interaction feels structured instead of random.
apollo.your_role: I defined the visual rules, interaction feel, and rendering logic for the system.
highlights: Focused on symmetry, structure, and precision in the visual output.
Used mathematically driven rules to guide how the visuals evolve.
Kept the interactions feeling controlled and intentional.
architecture: Rendering logic is driven by geometric constraints and patterned motion.
Interaction updates feed into a structured visual system rather than a purely chaotic one.
Animation timing emphasizes rhythm, balance, and clarity.
challenges: It is easy for mathematically driven visuals to feel sterile if the motion is too rigid.
Balance matters, because too much complexity breaks the sense of order.
Precision in interaction means small implementation decisions are very noticeable.
tradeoffs: More structure creates clarity, but can reduce spontaneity.
Tighter constraints improve harmony, but narrow the expressive range.
results: Built a generative visual piece where structure and symmetry are the core interaction themes.

faq.answer: Apollo is my structured generative visual piece. It focuses on symmetry, precision, and mathematically controlled motion.

aphrodite.title: Aphrodite
aphrodite.one_liner: Aphrodite is an interactive visual experience centered on fluidity, softness, and organic motion.
aphrodite.full_summary: I built Aphrodite as an interactive visual experience that leans into softness, fluidity, and aesthetic motion. It contrasts with more rigid systems by focusing on organic shapes, smooth transitions, and a feeling of responsiveness that is more sensual than structural.
aphrodite.why_it_matters: Aphrodite matters to me because it explores the opposite end of the design space from something like Apollo. The goal is not rigid precision, but beauty, responsiveness, and feel.
aphrodite.problem: Highly structured visual systems can feel cold. I wanted to explore a more organic interaction style where user input creates soft, responsive motion.
aphrodite.solution: I designed a real-time visual system around organic forms, smooth transitions, and interaction-driven motion so the output feels fluid and immersive.
aphrodite.your_role: I defined the interaction feel, motion language, and visual behavior for the piece.
highlights: Built around softness, fluidity, and aesthetic motion.
Used user input to influence the visuals in real time.
Focused on organic forms and smooth transitions over rigid geometry.
architecture: Real-time interaction continuously influences particle and shader-driven visuals.
Motion logic prioritizes smoothness and organic transformation.
Rendering emphasizes atmosphere and responsiveness.
challenges: Organic visuals can quickly become muddy if the motion language is not disciplined.
Softness still needs enough structure to feel intentional.
Real-time responsiveness matters because the visual feel depends on it.
tradeoffs: More fluidity improves atmosphere, but can reduce visual clarity.
Organic motion feels expressive, but it is harder to control precisely.
results: Built an interactive visual system that prioritizes softness, fluid motion, and aesthetic responsiveness.

faq.answer: Aphrodite is my fluid visual piece. It focuses on organic motion, smooth transitions, and a softer interaction style than my more structured work.

hermes.title: Hermes
hermes.one_liner: Hermes is a fast, reactive interaction system focused on speed, feedback, and responsiveness.
hermes.full_summary: I built Hermes as an interaction system where the main theme is speed. The goal is to make the system feel alive through immediate feedback, tight event handling, and motion that reacts clearly and quickly to user input.
hermes.why_it_matters: Hermes matters to me because responsiveness is one of the fastest ways a system communicates quality. This project explores how immediate feedback changes the feel of an interaction.
hermes.problem: Interactive systems often feel flat when input and response are loosely coupled. I wanted to explore what happens when reaction speed becomes the central design principle.
hermes.solution: I built a reactive system that emphasizes tight feedback loops, event-driven updates, and motion that responds immediately to user actions.
hermes.your_role: I designed the response behavior, event flow, and motion system.
highlights: Focused on making the system feel fast and alive.
Reduced the gap between input and visible response.
Used immediate motion feedback as the core interaction language.
architecture: User input feeds directly into a reactive event-driven system.
Motion logic is tuned for immediate visible feedback.
The interaction design emphasizes clarity through speed.
challenges: Fast interactions can feel noisy if feedback is not carefully designed.
Responsiveness has to improve clarity rather than just creating motion.
Small delays become much more noticeable when speed is the whole point.
tradeoffs: Aggressive responsiveness feels energetic, but it can become overwhelming.
Simpler motion improves clarity, but can reduce expressive range.
results: Built a reactive interaction piece where speed and responsiveness are the core design ideas.

faq.answer: Hermes is my reactive interaction piece. It is about speed, event-driven feedback, and making the system feel immediately responsive.

kronos.title: Kronos
kronos.one_liner: Kronos is a hand-tracking interactive particle system inspired by time and destruction.
kronos.full_summary: I built Kronos as a hand-tracking interactive particle system where computer vision turns hand movement into forces inside a physics-based visual environment. Users can manipulate the particles in real time, so the piece feels like a blend of physical simulation and direct bodily control.
kronos.why_it_matters: Kronos matters to me because it combines computer vision, physics simulation, and real-time rendering into one interaction loop.
kronos.problem: I wanted an interactive visual system where human motion does more than trigger effects. It should physically shape the environment in real time.
kronos.solution: I used hand tracking to detect motion and translate it into forces that drive a particle simulation rendered in real time.
kronos.your_role: I designed the interaction loop, computer-vision hookup, and particle behavior.
highlights: Tracked hand movement with computer vision.
Mapped motion into forces inside a particle simulation.
Let users manipulate a physics-based visual environment directly in real time.
architecture: MediaPipe detects hand movement and position in real time.
The input is transformed into force signals for the particle system.
A physics-based renderer updates the environment continuously in response to the user.
challenges: Computer-vision input is noisy, so the interaction has to stay stable.
Physics simulation has to remain responsive while still looking rich.
The mapping from hand motion to particle behavior needs to feel intuitive.
tradeoffs: Heavier physics improves visual richness, but can hurt responsiveness.
More sensitive hand tracking feels expressive, but can become unstable.
results: Built a real-time hand-tracked particle system driven by computer vision and physics.

faq.answer: Kronos is my hand-tracked particle system. It uses computer vision to turn hand motion into forces inside a real-time physics-based visual environment.
